taxonomy.label: processes
taxonomy.description: Fundamental carrier-flow capabilities the tool can represent, defined by their mathematical role rather than by named technologies. `Carriers` are the energy or non-energy commodities that flow between processes (e.g. electricity, heat, hydrogen, CO2, water, materials).

members.label: boundary exchange
members.description: Carriers can enter or leave the system across its boundary at a defined cost and availability (e.g. fuel supply, primary resource extraction, imports/exports to unmodelled regions).

members.label: one to one
members.description: A single in-flowing carrier can be converted to a single out-flowing carrier (e.g. power plants, electrolysers without heat recovery).

members.label: multi carrier io
members.description: A single conversion process can have several in-flowing and/or out-flowing carriers at fixed ratios (e.g. back-pressure CHP, fixed heat-recovery fractions).

members.label: flexible ratio
members.description: The ratio between a conversion process's flows can be a decision variable within a feasible operating region (e.g. extraction-condensing CHP, heat pumps serving heat and cooling).

members.label: temporal transfer
members.description: Carriers can be moved in time, linking system states across timesteps (e.g. storage).

members.label: spatial transfer
members.description: Carriers can be moved between regions as continuous flow subject to transfer-capacity limits, without network physics.

members.label: delayed transfer
members.description: Carriers can flow in space with a time delay between injection and withdrawal (e.g. river flows, district-heating transit).

members.label: buffered transfer
members.description: Carriers can flow in space with an endogenous in-transit inventory that accumulates over time (e.g. pipeline linepack).

members.label: discrete transport
members.description: Carriers can be moved in space in discrete packets with loading/unloading decisions (e.g. shipping, trucking, rail).

members.label: state changing transfer
members.description: A carrier can be moved at discrete physical state levels, with conversion between levels en route (e.g. heat-network temperature levels).

members.label: inelastic
members.description: A fixed quantity of a carrier can be consumed by a demand process whose in-flow can be constrained like any other process flow.

members.label: price responsive
members.description: The consumed quantity can be decided against willingness-to-pay (e.g. demand bids, stepwise/linear demand curves).

members.label: mobile storage
members.description: A consuming process can have embedded storage whose network attachment and availability vary in space and time (e.g. electric vehicles).

groups.label: conversion
groups.description: Carriers can be transformed into other carriers within the system boundary (e.g. power plants, electrolysers, heat pumps, CO2 capture).

groups.label: explicit demand
groups.description: Carriers can be consumed by explicit processes with their own balances and constraints, rather than by a fixed exogenous profile.

taxonomy.label: network
taxonomy.description: Flows can be coupled by the physics of the transporting medium, beyond the capacity limits of `processes.spatial_transfer`.

members.label: dc opf
members.description: DC optimal power flow can be modelled.

members.label: ac opf
members.description: Linearised AC optimal power flow can be modelled.

members.label: unbalanced flows
members.description: Unbalanced (asymmetric phase) flows can be modelled (e.g. linearised DistFlow).

members.label: ptdf
members.description: Supplied Power Transfer Distribution Factor <PTDF> limits can be applied, relating branch flows to nodal injections (e.g. with single or distributed slack).

members.label: outage factors
members.description: Supplied Line/Branch Outage Distribution Factor <LODF/BODF> limits can be applied, relating branch flows to the outage of another branch.

members.label: generic constraints
members.description: Built-in transmission constraint objects can be defined with user-supplied coefficients (e.g. flowgates, interfaces).

members.label: thermal
members.description: Thermal (branch flow magnitude) limits can be applied.

members.label: phase angle
members.description: Phase-angle difference limits between connected buses can be applied.

members.label: losses
members.description: Branch losses can vary with flow, rather than being a fixed transfer efficiency (e.g. piecewise-linear or quadratic loss approximations).

members.label: transformers
members.description: Transformers (tap ratio, fixed phase shift) and shunt elements can be represented.

members.label: facts devices
members.description: Controllable flow devices whose setting is a decision variable can be represented (e.g. optimised phase-shifting transformers, Flexible AC Transmission System <FACTS> devices).

members.label: hvdc converters
members.description: Rectifiers, inverters, and HVDC converter stations can be represented.

members.label: linearised flow
members.description: Nodal pressure/head can be a decision variable that couples flows through a linearised pressure-drop relationship, with limits on that state (e.g. minimum/maximum nodal pressure).

members.label: composition tracking
members.description: A single transfer asset can carry a mixture whose constituents are balanced individually, with limits on the resulting blend (e.g. hydrogen blend fraction, Wobbe index).

groups.label: power flow
groups.description: Electrical network physics can be represented.

groups.label: hydraulic flow
groups.description: Pressure-driven networks can be represented for carriers transported through pipes (e.g. methane, hydrogen, CO2, district heat, water).

taxonomy.label: decisions
taxonomy.description: Fidelity of the decisions made in the optimisation problem.

members.label: exogenous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be fixed in the input data (e.g. for dispatch-only modelling).

members.label: continuous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be a continuous decision variable, optionally bounded by a maximum (e.g. PV capacity up to a land-use limit).

members.label: integer investment exogenous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be built as a whole number of fixed-size units or blocks, with the number of units as an integer decision variable (e.g. nuclear units of fixed size).

members.label: integer investment continuous capacity
members.description: Asset capacity can be a continuous decision variable, with the decision to invest a binary or integer decision variable (e.g. individually tracked gas turbines of variable size).

members.label: multi period
members.description: Capacity can be decided over several investment periods rather than once for the whole horizon.

members.label: retrofit
members.description: Modifications to an existing asset can be invested in endogenously, changing its technical parameters or costs rather than adding standalone capacity (e.g. CO2 capture, efficiency upgrades, fuel switching).

members.label: endogenous retirement
members.description: Existing capacity can be retired early as a decision variable, rather than only at the end of a fixed lifetime.

members.label: unit commitment
members.description: Assets can be committed as discrete units and then economically dispatched.

members.label: maintenance scheduling
members.description: Asset maintenance / outage schedules can be derived endogenously, co-optimised with operation.

groups.label: investment
groups.description: How investment in asset capacity can be decided: the variable type of the capacity decision and the kinds of investment decision available.

groups.label: operation
groups.description: The resolution at which asset operation can be represented.

taxonomy.label: constraints
taxonomy.description: Limits on investment and operating decisions, split by the model dimension a limit engages, its functional form, and specific use-cases.

members.label: investment
members.description: The capacity or number of units added or retired within an investment period can be bounded above and/or below (e.g. minimum viable project size, maximum units built per year).

members.label: availability derating
members.description: An asset's flow or stored level can be bounded within a timestep by a time-varying fraction of its capacity (e.g. renewable capacity factors, seasonal de-rating, storage level limits).

members.label: minimum stable level
members.displayName: temporal > pointwise > operation > minimum stable level
members.description: A committed asset's flow can be bounded below by a minimum stable level, so that it either operates at or above that level or is off. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: forced offline
members.description: An asset can be required to be off in given timesteps (e.g. planned outage windows). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: forced online
members.description: An asset can be required to be on in given timesteps (e.g. must-run units). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: availability window
members.description: The investment periods in which an asset may be built or retired can be restricted (e.g. lead times, earliest commissioning dates).

members.label: relative build rate
members.displayName: temporal > sequential > investment > relative build rate
members.description: Capacity added in a period can be limited relative to earlier additions or installed capacity (e.g. technology growth limits).

members.label: technical lifetime
members.description: Capacity built in one period can be forced out of service a fixed number of periods later (e.g. end of technical life).

members.label: ramping
members.description: The change in an asset's flow between consecutive timesteps can be limited within its normal operating range.

members.label: start shut trajectory
members.displayName: temporal > sequential > operation > start shut trajectory
members.description: The flow trajectory while an asset starts up or shuts down can be limited separately from its normal operating range (e.g. run-up rates, start profiles). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: commitment duration
members.description: The number of consecutive timesteps an asset must or may remain in a commitment state can be limited (e.g. minimum up/down time). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: start consumption
members.description: A carrier in-flow can be required on a change of commitment state (e.g. start-up fuel). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: capacity target
members.description: Installed capacity can be bounded above or below, counted at nameplate or at a de-rating / capacity-credit factor (e.g. deployment targets, technical potential, planning reserve margins).

members.label: expansion budget
members.description: Accumulated investment spend can be bounded (e.g. a portfolio capital budget).

members.label: event count
members.description: The number of periods in which investment occurs can be limited, so that build-out is lumpy.

members.label: path dependent
members.description: An investment limit's bound can evolve endogenously with earlier investment (e.g. a learning curve raising deployable capacity in later periods).

members.label: flow volume
members.description: Total carrier in-/out-flow can be bounded over a period (e.g. annual throughput limits, hydro/fuel budgets, minimum capacity factor).

members.label: impact budget
members.description: Cumulative production or consumption of a user-definable non-carrier quantity can be bounded over a period (e.g. an annual CO2 cap, a water abstraction budget).

members.label: event count
members.description: The number of times a discrete event occurs can be limited over a period (e.g. maximum starts per year). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: state duration
members.description: The cumulative number of timesteps an asset spends in a given state can be limited over a period (e.g. total operating hours). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: path dependent
members.description: An operating limit's bound can evolve endogenously with earlier operation (e.g. battery degradation lowering available capacity).

members.label: investment
members.description: Investment can start from an existing asset stock, or target a user-defined end-state (e.g. backcasting).

members.label: operation
members.description: Initial or end-state operating values can be set, and their change between periods limited (e.g. start/end storage levels).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment limit can span several spatial units (e.g. a national deployment target).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating limit can span several spatial units (e.g. a system-wide emissions cap, a regional self-sufficiency requirement).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment limit can span several assets (e.g. a combined technology capacity target, land-use competition).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating limit can span several assets (e.g. a combined generation limit for a technology).

members.label: dedicated flow routing
members.description: Carrier out-flow from one asset can be reserved as in-flow to specific other assets, rather than pooled at the node (e.g. fuel stockpiling, hydro cascades).

members.label: investment
members.description: A linear relationship can link several investment decision variables (e.g. storage energy-to-power ratio envelopes).

members.label: operation
members.description: A linear relationship can link several operating decision variables (e.g. CHP heat-power operating regions).

members.label: investment
members.description: A quadratic constraint can involve an investment decision variable.

members.label: operation
members.description: A quadratic constraint can involve an operating decision variable (e.g. quadratic loss terms).

members.label: investment
members.description: A non-linear constraint can involve an investment decision variable (e.g. pipeline throughput scaling with diameter).

members.label: operation
members.description: A non-linear constraint can involve an operating decision variable (e.g. part-load efficiency, hydro head effects).

members.label: unserved demand
members.description: Demand can go unserved at a penalty cost (value of lost load <VOLL>).

members.label: online headroom
members.description: A requirement can be met from spare capability on running assets (e.g. spinning reserve, frequency regulation).

members.label: standby capability
members.description: A requirement can be met from offline assets that can start within a defined response time (e.g. non-spinning reserve). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: inertia
members.description: A requirement can be held on synchronised rotational energy rather than on power headroom (e.g. minimum system inertia).

members.label: contingency constrained
members.description: The optimisation can be constrained to remain feasible after the loss of individual components (e.g. N-1 security-constrained optimal power flow, loss of a compressor station).

members.label: loss of load
members.displayName: probabilistic reliability limit > loss of load
members.description: A loss-of-load-probability <LOLP> limit can be applied.

members.label: unserved energy
members.description: An expected-energy-not-served <EENS> limit can be applied.

members.label: soft constraints
members.description: Any user-defined or built-in constraint can be made soft through a generic slack-plus-penalty mechanism.

groups.label: scope
groups.description: Which model dimensions a limit engages. A limit engaging several dimensions is recorded under each of them (e.g. a fleet-wide annual cap is both `temporal` and `assets`).

groups.label: functional form
groups.description: The mathematical form of relationships between decision variables in constraints, and hence the problem class handed to the solver.

groups.label: reliability
groups.description: Requirements against component failure or short-term imbalance can be imposed within the optimisation.

taxonomy.label: cost
taxonomy.description: Costs attached to investment and operating decisions as objective terms, beyond cost varying linearly with a decision variable.

members.label: investment
members.description: A cost can be incurred on a change in installed capacity between investment periods (e.g. a decommissioning charge).

members.label: ramping
members.description: A cost can be incurred in proportion to the change in an asset's flow between timesteps.

members.label: start up
members.description: A cost can be incurred each time an asset starts up. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: shut down
members.description: A cost can be incurred each time an asset shuts down. Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: start state dependent
members.displayName: temporal > sequential > operation > start state dependent
members.description: Start-up cost can vary with how long the asset has been offline (e.g. hot / warm / cold starts). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: investment
members.description: A capital cost coefficient can change with cumulative deployment (e.g. an endogenous learning curve).

members.label: operation
members.description: An operating cost coefficient can change with cumulative prior operation (e.g. maintenance cost rising with running hours).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment cost can span several spatial units (e.g. a corridor reinforcement charge).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating cost can span several spatial units (e.g. a charge on a region's aggregate net imports).

members.label: investment
members.description: A single investment cost can span several assets (e.g. a shared site or grid connection charge).

members.label: operation
members.description: A single operating cost can span several assets (e.g. a contract priced on combined output).

members.label: investment
members.description: A capital cost can be incurred per asset purchased, irrespective of capacity (e.g. land purchase). Usually requires `decisions.investment.integer_investment_...`.

members.label: operation
members.description: A cost can be incurred for each timestep an asset is committed, irrespective of its flow (e.g. no-load cost). Usually requires `decisions.operation.unit_commitment`.

members.label: investment
members.description: Capital cost per unit of capacity can vary with capacity (e.g. economies of scale).

members.label: operation
members.description: Operating cost per unit of flow can vary with the level of that flow (e.g. heat-rate curves, stepwise price-quantity offer bands).

members.label: investment
members.description: Costs can be applied to deviation from a reference investment level (e.g. a firm-capacity rebate).

members.label: operation
members.description: Costs can be applied to deviation from a reference operating level (e.g. incr/decr offers around a day-ahead schedule, redispatch).

members.label: annuitisation
members.description: Overnight capital cost can be spread across an asset's economic life using a discount rate (e.g. weighted average cost of capital <WACC>).

members.label: fiscal treatment
members.description: Tax and depreciation arrangements can adjust annuitised cost (e.g. investment tax credits, depreciation schedules).

members.label: period discounting
members.description: Costs in later investment periods can be discounted to present value in the objective.

groups.label: scope
groups.description: Which model dimensions a cost term engages. A cost engaging several dimensions is recorded under each of them (e.g. a charge on a fleet's combined running hours is both `temporal` and `assets`).

groups.label: functional form
groups.description: How a cost can vary with the decision variable it attaches to, beyond the linear baseline.

groups.label: time value
groups.description: Costs can be adjusted for when they are incurred and how they are financed.

taxonomy.label: objective
taxonomy.description: The objective function can extend beyond minimising a single linear cost.

members.label: quadratic
members.description: Quadratic objective terms can be passed natively to the solver (e.g. welfare maximisation with linear demand curves).

members.label: multi objective weighted
members.description: Multiple objective terms can be combined via user-set weights.

members.label: multi objective pareto
members.description: Pareto-optimal solution sets can be generated across objectives (e.g. epsilon-constraint).

members.label: tie breaking
members.description: Degenerate solutions can be resolved by a documented rule rather than solver arbitrariness (e.g. small penalties on zero-cost variables).

taxonomy.label: edge effects
taxonomy.description: Distortions caused by model boundaries and linearisation can be mitigated endogenously.

members.label: time operational
members.description: End-of-horizon operational effects can be mitigated (e.g. cyclic storage levels, terminal value of stored energy).

members.label: time financial
members.description: End-of-horizon financial effects can be mitigated (e.g. residual value of assets outliving the horizon).

members.label: energy balance
members.description: Spurious energy destruction from simultaneous in- and out-flow of a lossy transfer/storage asset can be prevented.

taxonomy.label: actors
taxonomy.description: Heterogeneous decision-making actors can be represented, beyond a single central planner.

members.label: portfolio
members.description: Actor asset portfolios with their own constraints and costs can be represented (e.g. capital limits per company).

members.label: heuristic markup
members.description: Strategic price/offer markups can be applied by heuristic or index-based rules (e.g. Residual Supply Index <RSI>-driven markups).

members.label: distributed objectives
members.description: Per-actor objectives can be represented within the system-level optimisation (e.g. prosumer decisions).

members.label: equilibrium
members.description: Market equilibrium across actors with competing objectives can be computed (e.g. Cournot-Nash via complementarity or bi-level formulations).

taxonomy.label: uncertainty
taxonomy.description: The decision problem can be restructured to account for parametric or structural uncertainty.

members.label: two stage stochastic
members.description: Two-stage stochastic optimisation can be performed (e.g. investment under uncertainty).

members.label: multi stage stochastic
members.description: Multi-stage stochastic optimisation can be performed, with decisions revised as uncertainty resolves (e.g. hydro scheduling under uncertain inflows).

members.label: risk aversion
members.description: Risk measures can be applied in the objective or constraints of a stochastic optimisation (e.g. Conditional Value at Risk <CVaR>).

members.label: robust optimisation
members.description: Worst-case cost can be minimised over an uncertainty set.

members.label: near optimal
members.description: Alternative near-optimal solutions can be generated (e.g. Modelling to Generate Alternatives <MGA>).

taxonomy.label: model definition
taxonomy.description: How the model's parameter space and dimensions can be shaped, grouped, and reused.

members.label: configurable dimensions
members.description: The dimensionality of an asset parameter or cost can be configured by the user from a set of tool-defined dimensions.

members.label: extensible dimensions
members.description: A dimension not natively defined by the tool can be introduced by the user, and parameters and math indexed over it (e.g. a custom cohort axis).

members.label: dimension groups
members.description: Dimension members can be tagged into named, potentially overlapping groups, for use in constraints, aggregation, and analysis (e.g. "coastal assets" spanning several technologies and nodes).

members.label: component templating
members.description: Components can inherit parameters from a shared template, including programmatic generation of components from a template (e.g. an abstract technology definition, auto-cloned vintages).

taxonomy.label: math
taxonomy.description: Access to, and user extension of, the underlying mathematical formulation.

members.label: formulation transparency
members.description: The tool's mathematical formulation can be inspected (e.g. rendered equations traceable to the built problem).

members.label: problem file export
members.description: The built optimisation problem can be exported in standard formats (e.g. LP/MPS).

members.label: dual extraction
members.description: Constraint duals can be extracted from the solved problem.

members.label: piecewise formulation
members.description: Piecewise constructs are available to build non-linear relationships in the math (e.g. SOS2 constraints).

members.label: user defined math
members.description: Users can define their own constraints, variables, and objective expression.

taxonomy.label: tractability
taxonomy.description: The computational cost of building and solving the problem can be reduced, trading exactness for speed.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Timesteps or investment periods can be merged contiguously (e.g. hourly to daily).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Bordering spatial units can be merged into contiguous zones (e.g. buses to bidding zones).

members.label: temporal
members.description: A full timeseries can be represented by non-contiguous typical periods or duration curves.

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial units can be clustered by likeness rather than adjacency (e.g. by resource quality).

members.label: assets
members.description: Individual assets can be aggregated into asset groups.

members.label: scenarios
members.description: A scenario ensemble can be reduced to a weighted representative set.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Inter-temporal features can be linked across typical periods (e.g. storage levels).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Inter-spatial features can be linked across discontiguous zones.

members.label: spatial
members.description: Network elements can be equivalenced (e.g. Ward or Kron reduction).

members.label: assets
members.description: A chain of interconnected assets can be collapsed into a single component.

members.label: temporal
members.description: Timesteps or investment periods can be filtered out (e.g. to a user-selected study window).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial units can be filtered out (e.g. below a voltage level).

members.label: assets
members.description: Assets can be filtered out (e.g. by node or carrier).

members.label: scenarios
members.description: Scenarios can be filtered out.

members.label: formulation
members.description: The mathematical fidelity of the same attribute can differ across the model's scope (e.g. unit commitment near-term, continuous dispatch beyond).

members.label: temporal
members.description: Temporal resolution can vary across another dimension (e.g. hourly in a focus region, daily elsewhere).

members.label: spatial
members.description: Spatial resolution can vary across another dimension (e.g. nodal near-term, zonal beyond).

members.label: assets
members.description: Asset resolution can vary across another dimension (e.g. individual assets in a focus region, groups elsewhere).

members.label: scenarios
members.description: Scenario resolution can vary across another dimension (e.g. a scenario tree branching more finely near-term).

members.label: linearised unit commitment
members.description: Unit commitment can be approximated with continuous commitment variables.

members.label: convex relaxation
members.description: A non-convex relationship in the tool's own formulation can be convexified (e.g. second-order-cone relaxation of AC power flow).

members.label: function conversion
members.description: User-supplied non-linear functions can be converted automatically into valid model inputs (e.g. piecewise segments).

members.label: constraint screening
members.description: Constraints unlikely to bind can be omitted or lazily added.

members.label: decomposition
members.description: The problem can be split into coordinated sub-problems solved iteratively or in parallel (e.g. Benders, progressive hedging, Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming <SDDP>).

members.label: numeric scaling
members.description: Data can be scaled to reduce numerical instability in the solver.

groups.label: dimension reduction
groups.description: The number of members along a dimension can be reduced automatically, uniformly across all other dimensions.

groups.label: variable fidelity
groups.description: The fidelity of the same attribute/dimension can differ across the model's scope.

groups.label: reformulation
groups.description: The built problem or its solution algorithm can be reformulated to reduce solve cost.

taxonomy.label: orchestration
taxonomy.description: Multiple complete runs can be coordinated by tool-managed workflows.

members.label: scenario runs
members.description: Discrete, named scenarios can be executed in batch with collated outputs.

members.label: sampled runs
members.description: Run ensembles can be executed over a sampled uncertainty space with collated outputs (e.g. Monte Carlo).

members.label: investment
members.description: Investment can be optimised sequentially per period or set of periods (e.g. myopic foresight).

members.label: operation
members.description: Dispatch can be optimised sequentially per set of timesteps (e.g. rolling horizon).

members.label: fidelity sequence
members.description: Models of the same system at different fidelity can be run in sequence, passing data between them (e.g. capacity expansion followed by unit-commitment dispatch).

members.label: market sequence
members.description: Models of successive market stages can be run with bidirectional data exchange (e.g. interleaved day-ahead / real-time runs).

members.label: convergence iteration
members.description: Runs can be repeated, exchanging data, until relationships not representable in a single problem converge (e.g. iterating on line reactances).

groups.label: coupled models
groups.description: Two or more model runs can be executed with tool-managed data exchange between them.

taxonomy.label: io
taxonomy.description: Data formats, conventions, and mechanisms for moving model input/output data.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be provided in this format.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written in this format.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be provided in this format.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written in this format.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be read from a database.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written to a database.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be read from remote storage.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be written to remote storage.

members.label: input
members.description: Input data can be loaded lazily.

members.label: output
members.description: Output data can be streamed rather than held fully in memory.

members.label: input
members.description: Standardised input data can be accepted.

members.label: output
members.description: Outputs can follow a standard.

groups.label: plain text
groups.description: Data can be handled in human-readable, version-control-friendly text formats (e.g. CSV, JSON, YAML).

groups.label: binary
groups.description: Data can be handled in binary formats (e.g. Excel, NetCDF, HDF5, Parquet).

groups.label: database
groups.description: Data can be handled in databases.

groups.label: remote storage
groups.description: Data can be read from / written to remote storage (e.g. object stores).

groups.label: lazy loading
groups.description: Data larger than memory can be handled out-of-core.

groups.label: standardised
groups.description: Data can follow a community-recognised convention, ontology, or network-data format (e.g. Open Energy Ontology <OEO>, IAMC template, Common Information Model <CIM>, PSSE RAW).

taxonomy.label: preprocessing
taxonomy.description: Parameters can be derived from user-defined input data before running the model.

members.label: download
members.description: Data can be downloaded within the tool from an external source.

members.label: model catalogue
members.description: Pre-built models can be retrieved from a catalogue as starting points.

members.label: resource conversion
members.description: Profiles can be derived from weather or resource data via physical response models (e.g. wind speed to capacity factor, temperature to heat demand).

members.label: forecasting
members.description: A profile can be scaled or reshaped to meet forecast targets (e.g. annual total or peak).

members.label: demand
members.description: Nodal demand can be distributed from an aggregate total.

members.label: network geometry
members.description: Line or pipeline lengths or routes can be derived from node coordinates.

members.label: scenario generation
members.description: Scenario ensembles can be generated from parameters or sampling rules.

members.label: input validation
members.description: Input data can be validated against expected structure and value ranges before a run.

groups.label: spatial distribution
groups.description: A parameter can be distributed spatially using other spatial parameters.

taxonomy.label: postprocessing
taxonomy.description: Analyses of model outputs that can be triggered by the tool.

members.label: capacity factor
members.description: Average output relative to capacity can be calculated.

members.label: operating hours
members.description: The number of timesteps an asset is running can be calculated.

members.label: binding hours
members.description: The number of timesteps an asset's flow is at its upper bound can be calculated (e.g. line congestion hours).

members.label: curtailment
members.description: Curtailment can be calculated.

members.label: marginal price

useCases.name: Bidding Zone Review
useCases.description: Model impact on energy system design, systemwide costs, and / or transmission system congestion of implementing new market mechanisms or updating existing ones. This could include bidding zone reviews; direct subsidies; feed-in-tariffs; contract auctions.
assumptions: A single target year is modelled. Generation, storage, and transmission capacities are fixed by the integrated resource plan (IRP) and network development plan (NDP); no investment decisions are made.
Several candidate bidding-zone configurations are compared, each formed by grouping the nodes of a detailed transmission grid model into zones.

For each configuration, the day-ahead market is cleared zonally using flow-based market coupling. Zone-to-line power transfer distribution factors (PTDFs) and critical network elements and contingencies (CNECs) are supplied as inputs.

The market schedule is redispatched on the nodal grid model (DC power flow, N-1 security). Deviations from the schedule is priced at redispatch offers, giving congestion and redispatch costs per configuration.
Thermal and hydro units are resolved individually, with unit commitment and stepwise bid curves, to represent day-ahead scheduling realistically.

The year is optimised in rolling windows of days to weeks (myopic foresight within the year), handing storage levels over between windows. Seasonal hydro storage is valued with water values from a longer-horizon run.
Only the power system is modelled. Other sectors enter as exogenous demand profiles and price-responsive demand bids.
Weather uncertainty is covered by running several historical climate years as separate deterministic scenarios rather than by stochastic optimisation.
Load shedding is allowed at the value of lost load (VOLL). Adequacy is not a decision criterion, so no probabilistic reliability limits are applied.
Configurations are assessed on socio-economic welfare, zonal price differences, cross-zonal capacities, congestion rents, redispatch volumes and costs, generator revenues, and CO2 emissions.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.

useCases.name: Integrated Resource Planning (IRP)
useCases.description: Create a set of high-level scenarios of e.g. 2050 decarbonised energy system designs for use in guiding policy implementation, creating procurement plans, and providing boundary conditions for investors, utilities, and local authorities to develop their own plans. Future scenarios account for full sector coupling and GHG emission accounting.
assumptions: Capacity expansion is optimised with perfect foresight over the full horizon (e.g. to 2050), with investment decisions every N (> 1) years and the existing fleet as the starting point.
Each investment period is represented by a contiguous timeseries that may be resampled (e.g. to 3-hourly).

The energy system is fully sector-coupled. Electricity, heat, transport, hydrogen, and gas demands, and conversion between these carriers, are represented, and GHG emissions are accounted for across all sectors.
The system is divided into a handful of regions (e.g. provinces or market zones) linked by transfer capacities for electricity and gas, without network physics.
Large units (e.g. nuclear, large hydro, thermal power plants) are built in discrete unit sizes. Distributed assets (e.g. wind, solar, rooftop PV) are grouped per region and resource class.

The thermal fleet is operated with linearised unit commitment (minimum stable level, ramping, minimum up/down times, start-up costs). This captures flexibility needs without integer commitment variables.

Existing plants retire at the end of their technical lifetime or earlier if uneconomic. New technologies are only available from given commissioning dates and are subject to per-period and relative build-rate limits.
Policy targets (e.g. economy-wide CO2 caps, renewable shares, technology-specific targets) are set as user-defined constraints that may span regions and subsets of technologies.
Generator contract arrangements (e.g. minimum/maximum annual dispatch obligations) are represented as annual volume limits.
A planning reserve margin on de-rated firm capacity and an operating reserve requirement are enforced. Load shedding is allowed at the value of lost load (VOLL).
Resource adequacy (LOLE, EENS, capacity credit of variable renewables) is assessed post hoc rather than constrained.
The preferred plans are validated in a chronological, hourly production-cost run with fixed capacities and full unit commitment.
Demand-side flexibility is represented by time-shiftable loads and smart charging of electric vehicles.
Hydro and other storage levels are cyclic within each period. The residual value of assets outliving the horizon is accounted for.
Hydro cascading and technology chaining internal to power plants is not represented.
Transmission and storage losses are fixed efficiencies, and there is no incentive to dump energy. So, "unphysical" energy destruction does not need to be mitigated against.
Sensitivity analysis is limited to a small set of named scenarios. Stochastic optimisation, Monte Carlo sampling, and near-optimal (MGA) analysis are not employed.
There is sufficient computational capacity to run the model at the defined spatio-temporal scope and resolution without decomposition.
Plans are compared on system net present value, levelised costs, marginal prices, emissions, and curtailment.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.

useCases.name: Network Development Plan (NDP) / Transmission Planning Process (TPP)
useCases.description: Create a set of detailed scenarios of e.g., 2050 transmission grid designs for use in guiding policy implementation and providing boundary conditions for investors, utilities, and local authorities to develop their own plans. The transmission plans will be optimized based on high-level scenarios of decarbonised energy system findings.
assumptions: Transmission expansion is optimised with perfect foresight across several investment years (e.g. 2030, 2035, 2040).
Generation capacities are fixed by the integrated resource plan (IRP) in each investment year.
Candidate projects include new AC circuits (discrete units), HVDC corridors (continuous size), and upgrades of existing circuits, each with an earliest commissioning date.
The grid is represented nodally with DC power flow, including thermal limits, transformers and phase-shifters, HVDC links and converters, flow-dependent losses, and N-1 security.
Voltage and reactive-power adequacy of the chosen plan is checked in separate AC load-flow studies, outside this optimisation.
Line impedances change with expansion, so the optimisation is iterated until flows and the chosen build are consistent.
For tractability, grids outside the study area and lower voltage levels are reduced or filtered out, and only contingencies likely to bind are included.
Assets are grouped, and only their dispatch is represented, not their unit commitment.
Contracted operating arrangements and regulated limits (e.g. on emissions) defined in the IRP are applied.
Each investment year is represented by an hourly (or resampled) timeseries. Different weather and demand years are used to stress-test the plan, but not as a formal Monte Carlo analysis.
Load shedding is allowed at the value of lost load (VOLL). Adequacy (LOLE, EENS) is a cost-benefit indicator computed post hoc, not a constraint.

Candidate projects are assessed with cost-benefit indicators, including socio-economic welfare, congestion rents, losses, CO2 emissions, curtailment, adequacy, transfer capacities, congestion hours, and project net present value.
Investment and storage horizon edge effects are ignored in the optimisation. Residual value is handled in the post- hoc project assessment.
User-defined constraints and decision variables may be required to represent one-off transmission system quirks.
Network data are taken from transmission system operator (TSO) grid models in standard formats. Outputs must be formatted and traceable for regulatory approval.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.

useCases.name: Policy Target Setting
useCases.description: Political exercise to set carbon emission pathways to meet future year targets
assumptions: The optimisation is run with perfect foresight over the full horizon, which spans multiple decades at 5-year resolution, starting from the existing asset stock.

The spatial scope is national and single-node. It could be multi-node at national resolution for a multinational study, but that is not chosen here. Imports and exports are exchanges across the system boundary.
Each year is represented by representative time slices (e.g. season x day/night/peak). Automated clustering into representative periods would also work but is not chosen here.
Storage is aggregated, and its level is linked across time slices.
The system is multi-carrier, including electricity, hydrogen, natural gas, heat, and oil products, with conversion between them (e.g. CHP, refineries).
Demands are end-use services (e.g. "vehicle km" for transport) met by conversion technologies, and they respond to price through elastic demand curves.
Extraction of domestic fossil resources is represented by assets, competing with imports, and is bounded by resource potentials.
Assets are always grouped. They are sub-grouped by cost and resource class in preprocessing and grouped back up in postprocessing.

Complex asset operating characteristics (unit commitment, ramping) are not represented. Assets have availability factors, and outages are covered by a reserve margin of de-rated dispatchable capacity.
Deployment is bounded by technology availability dates, technical lifetimes, per-period and relative growth limits, and technical potentials. Early retirement of fossil assets is a decision.
Emission caps per period, a cumulative carbon budget, and sector- or technology-specific targets are set by user-defined constraints on subsets of the system.
Endogenous learning is not used, as it distorts the model. Cost trajectories are exogenous.
Technology-specific discount rates (hurdle rates) represent consumer preferences on payback periods.
Marginal prices and shadow prices of targets (e.g. marginal abatement cost of CO2) are required to compare scenarios.
Sensitivity scenarios are run, but detailed sensitivity analysis and stochastic optimisation are beyond the scope of this study.
A GUI is necessary, particularly for outputs.

useCases.name: Asset portfolio investment plan
useCases.description: Create an asset portfolio investment plan as a private / public utility company. This plan will be guided by national / regional plans (IRPs, NDPs, etc.), the company's   current risk appetite, and any upcoming changes to market mechanisms / subsidies which may impact revenue.
assumptions: The utility's investment plan covers a 10-15 year horizon in annual or multi-year investment periods with perfect foresight.
Candidate projects are discrete decisions with project-specific sizes, a minimum viable size, and earliest commissioning dates.

The operating revenue of candidate portfolios is analysed with rolling-horizon market simulation over days to weeks (myopic foresight within the year), interleaving day-ahead and intra-day market stages.

Portfolio assets are resolved individually with unit commitment characteristics, including minimum stable level, ramp rates, start-up and shut-down trajectories, minimum up/down times, and start-up fuel.
Cost detail for portfolio assets includes hot/warm/cold start-up costs, no-load costs, and heat-rate curves, with non-linear operating and financial relationships piecewise linearised.
Maintenance windows are co-optimised with operation. Start and operating-hour limits from long-term service agreements are respected.
Hydro cascades are represented, including water travel times. So are multi-configuration plants (e.g. CCGT/CHP) with flexible operating regions.
Battery degradation is represented, as storage revenue over the horizon depends on it.

The rest of the system develops according to the scenarios in the integrated resource plan (IRP) and network development plan (NDP). It is resolved coarsely (zonal, grouped assets, linear dispatch), and competitors' bidding is approximated by heuristic markups.
Grid-connection limits for portfolio assets are imposed through PTDFs supplied by the transmission system operator. Nodal network physics is not represented.
A capital budget limits total investment across the portfolio. Company-level emission and renewable-capacity targets may apply.

Financial assessment uses the company's WACC, tax and depreciation, and asset-level revenue accounts. It includes settlement of PPAs, contracts-for-difference, and capacity obligations, as well as ancillary-service revenues.
Financial and operational horizon edge effects must be considered, as the portfolio includes storage.

Weather and market uncertainty are handled by two-stage stochastic optimisation (investment in the first stage) with a CVaR risk measure. It runs over a reduced set of sampled scenarios and may require decomposition.
Near-optimal alternative portfolios are generated to inform decision makers.
Externalities (loads, fuel and carbon prices, changes to asset capacities beyond the current portfolio) must be forecast over the next 10-15 years.
Users require a GUI to navigate model preparation, optimisation, and analysis.
